subject: penguin
pitch: An emperor penguin chick's proud parent. Glossy blue-black back and head, a crisp white belly blending into a warm golden-yellow patch at the neck and ear, a long slender beak with an orange-pink stripe, stubby flippers held slightly out, and big black feet. A fluffy grey chick peeks out from between its feet.
reasoning:
I'm planning to model an emperor penguin adult (~1.1m) with a fluffy grey chick (~0.3-0.4m) peeking from between its feet, using the SDK to build this scene as a TypeScript module.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton hierarchy for the adult — root hips joint, spine chain up through chest and neck to head, plus separate upper and lower beak joints for the mouth.

For the limbs, I'm planning flipper chains using a "wing" role and leg chains with hip, knee, ankle, and toe joints, with flat webbed feet modeled as extruded slabs pointing forward since the legs themselves are short and mostly hidden in the body.

The chick will get its own joint hierarchy, likely parented under the adult's root as a separate "chickRoot" chain.

I'm considering how to achieve a fluffy look for the chick without SVG textures—maybe tufted cards or a mottled, spiky sphere—and now I'm mapping out the core builder API calls I'll rely on, like joint and chain creation with their parameters, to keep everything correct since I can't test the code directly.

The `root` getter bakes and returns `ctx.root`, so the module structure imports the builder and paint utilities, defines a meta export, and the default export builds the penguin via `b.root`. For colors, I'm thinking through how to approximate glossy blue-black plumage given the fixed roughness/metalness material system—since gloss can't be set per part, I may need to fake sheen through paint variation rather than actual material properties.

For the belly, I'll use crisp white, and the golden-yellow ear/neck patch needs a warm orange-yellow tone. The beak is trickier: it needs a dark base with an orange-pink stripe, so I'm considering whether to paint that stripe procedurally based on the point's position along the beak, since the upper and lower mandibles are separate parts each needing their own paint function tied to local geometry.

Feet stay black, and the chick gets a soft downy grey with a paler belly to match the fluffy look of emperor penguin chicks. For the overall body shape, I'm leaning toward a lathed egg/capsule form with a single mesh, splitting the back and belly coloring through a normal-based countershade paint rather than separate geometry.

For the paint logic, I want to shade the back-facing surface blue-black and the front-facing chest white, using normal.z as the main discriminator, with position blended in for softer transitions. The head needs black on top and sides, golden-yellow patches near the ears/upper neck, and a white-to-cream throat and chest consistent with real emperor penguin coloring.

For the body shape itself, I'm considering whether a lathe (surface of revolution) gives too round a cross-section, and exploring whether a sweep with a non-uniform radius function could flatten the body silhouette more naturally along its vertical axis.

Working through the cross product math, I find the local normal points backward (-Z) and the binormal points toward -X, meaning rx maps to the side (left-right) axis and ry to the front-back depth axis. Since the penguin body is symmetric, the exact sign doesn't matter for the sweep frames to work correctly.

For the rigging, I'm considering whether the body needs a bendable spine chain or can stay rigid since penguins are mostly upright. A spine chain running from hip through chest to neck/head could drive the body loft via the `bone` option, or alternatively I could sweep directly along the spine chain with a radius function varying by parameter t.

I'm now sketching actual proportions: feet at ground level, legs rising to a narrow waist around y=0.1, widening through the belly at y=0.35-0.6, tapering at the neck near y=0.85, with the head sitting around y=0.97-1.1. Emperor penguins are quite tall and slender overall, so I'm working out realistic meter-scale dimensions for each body segment.

For the head itself, I'm considering shaping it as a lathed profile revolved around the Y axis to get a rounded, slightly pointed form approximating the skull and beak base.

Then I need to work out the paint logic for coloring the head regions: gold cheek patches positioned at the sides near the ears, using distance checks from a defined center point and radius to blend the coloring smoothly rather than with hard edges.

Working out the body color zones: dark blue-black on the back, white smoothed across the front chest/belly, and gold patches blending in on the sides of the neck and ears, using smoothstep masks based on surface normal and height to blend the transitions naturally.

I'm checking the SDK exports to confirm `mix` resolves to the paint color blending function rather than the bone-weight mix, so I can safely blend colors between zones using tuples or paint values directly.

The paint's `at(p, n, s)` is evaluated in model/root space during bake using the mesh's bind pose, since no poses are applied yet, so the coordinates I'm computing against are straightforward. I'm now thinking through the paint sheet resolution and how charts get packed within the 2048 texture.

With many separate paint parts (body, head, flippers, feet, beak, chick), the chart count will be fairly high since curved surfaces split into several charts each, so packing efficiency drops a bit but the density still comes out around a millimeter per texel, well under the max — should be fine. Now I'm placing the fluffy grey chick, roughly 0.35m tall, tucked beneath the adult's belly peeking out between its feet.

For the fluffy chick texture, I'm weighing options — SVG textures risk rendering blank if rasterization isn't awaited, which would make alphaTest cards disappear. Safer might be building the fluff from small spiky grey tuft shapes instead of relying on texture cards.

Scattering dozens of small cone "tufts" across the chick's spherical body surface using surface scatter points and sticking cone geometry at each hit point, oriented along the normals, seems like a solid deterministic approach — maybe 60 tufts, well within part and triangle budgets for a low-poly look.

Scattering needs filtering to avoid hidden points like the sphere's bottom. For the penguin's details I'm planning a dark glossy eye with a highlight, the golden ear patch, and the beak, plus thinking through posture — chest puffed, head held high — to convey a proud parent look.

For the chick peeking between the feet, I'm deciding whether it needs its own joint hierarchy or can just be built as attached parts without explicit bones, defaulting to the nearest joint.

I think giving the chick its own joint, parented to the root hips joint, makes more sense so it moves as a unit with the parent body. Now I'm sketching the overall joint hierarchy, starting with the root hips joint positioned near the pelvis as the base for the spine chain and chick attachment.

Working out the spine chain's catmull path from hips through chest to neck base, and figuring out how the joint count and naming correspond to the path's knot spans so the tip joint lands correctly at the chain's end.

Then I'm planning to simplify the rig structure: a spine chain from hips to chest, a neck chain continuing to the head base, a separate head joint parented to the neck tip, and a jaw joint parented to the head for the beak hinge, making sure all joint names stay unique and valid.

For the feet placement, I'm setting left foot origin at x=0.085 and right at x=-0.085, both with toes extending forward to about z=0.2 for the "big feet" look, while keeping the legs tucked near the body center so the chick can nestle between them around z=0.1.

Positioning the chick low and centered so its head emerges from under the belly fold, between the legs, with the body partly tucked beneath the parent's front — that reads as the classic brooding pose. Checking the loft's path-frame math now -- making sure width/height interpolation along the spine stays consistent with arc-length-based parameterization so the cross-sections line up correctly front-to-back and side-to-side.

I'm considering whether the first spine joint should coincide with the root hips joint or stay separate.

Since there's a requirement for exactly one root joint, I realize I need to create "hips" as the explicit root first, then set it as the parent for the spine chain -- but that risks a redundant zero-length bone if the chain's first joint duplicates the hips position, so I'm thinking through how to avoid that duplication.

Checking how weights resolve for a bare path vs needing a joint confirms a chain can't be the first element without a preceding joint — I need a root joint before the spine chain starts.
